evidence.snippet: Haploinsufficiency of PAFAH1B1 is responsible for the characteristic lissencephaly in MDS.
evidence.explanation: Directly attributes the characteristic lissencephaly to PAFAH1B1 (LIS1) haploinsufficiency.

evidence.snippet: Lis1 haploinsufficiency is shown here to also result in reduced filamentous actin at the leading edge of migrating neurons, associated with upregulation of RhoA and downregulation of Rac1 and Cdc42 activity.
evidence.explanation: Mouse data link Lis1 haploinsufficiency to a cytoskeletal migration defect via dysregulated Rho GTPase signaling.

steps/2.description: Loss of one PAFAH1B1 (LIS1) allele reduces LIS1 protein dosage. LIS1 regulates the cytoplasmic dynein motor and microtubule dynamics that drive nucleokinesis (nuclear translocation) of migrating neurons. LIS1 haploinsufficiency also reduces filamentous actin at the leading edge of migrating neurons through dysregulated Rho GTPase activity, impairing motility. Structural studies place type-1 lissencephaly mutations directly within the dynein-LIS1 interface.

evidence.snippet: Mice heterozygous with respect to both genes have more severe migration defects than single heterozygotes.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that combined Ywhae and Pafah1b1 deficiency produces a more severe migration defect, explaining the greater severity of MDLS versus isolated lissencephaly.

evidence.snippet: Similar to LIS1, deficiency of 14-3-3epsilon results in mislocalization of NUDEL and LIS1, consistent with reduction of cytoplasmic dynein function.
evidence.explanation: Provides the molecular mechanism by which 14-3-3 epsilon loss converges on reduced dynein function in the LIS1/NDEL1 pathway.

steps/3.description: Co-deletion of YWHAE (encoding 14-3-3 epsilon) augments the neuronal migration defect. 14-3-3 epsilon binds CDK5/p35-phosphorylated NDEL1 (NUDEL) and sustains its phosphorylation; its loss mislocalizes NDEL1 and LIS1, reducing cytoplasmic dynein function. Mice doubly deficient for Ywhae and Pafah1b1 have more severe migration defects than single heterozygotes, providing a molecular explanation for why YWHAE-including deletions cause the more severe Miller-Dieker phenotype.

evidence.snippet: PIDD1-mutant organoids and MDLS organoids recapitulated the thickened cortex typical of human lissencephaly and demonstrated dysregulation of protein translation, metabolism and the mTOR pathway.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived MDLS organoids show mTOR pathway dysregulation alongside the recapitulated lissencephalic cortex.

evidence.snippet: A brain-selective activator of mTOR complex 1 prevented and reversed cellular and molecular defects in the lissencephaly organoids.
evidence.explanation: Supports mTOR hypoactivity as a causal, reversible contributor to the cellular phenotype in MDLS organoids.

steps/4.description: Cerebral organoids derived from individuals with the MDLS 17p13.3 microdeletion recapitulate the thickened lissencephalic cortex and show dysregulation of protein translation, metabolism, and the mTOR pathway. mTOR hypoactivity acts as a convergent molecular mechanism that contributes to the lissencephalic cortical phenotype rather than arising as a downstream consequence of it: a brain-selective mTORC1 activator prevented and reversed the cellular and molecular defects in these organoids, identifying mTOR hypoactivity as a causal, potentially targetable mechanism. This is a research-stage mechanism.

evidence.snippet: One hallmark feature of MDS is an unusually smooth brain surface due to abnormal neuronal migration during early brain development.
evidence.explanation: Connects the abnormal neuronal migration to the hallmark smooth cortical surface (lissencephaly).

evidence.snippet: We saw a cell migration defect that was rescued when we corrected the MDS causative chromosomal deletion and severe apoptosis of the founder neuroepithelial stem cells, accompanied by increased horizontal cell divisions.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived MDS iPSC cerebral organoids reproduce the neuronal migration defect and demonstrate that correcting the causative 17p13.3 deletion rescues it, alongside apoptosis of the founder neuroepithelial stem cells — human in vitro (organoid) mechanistic support for the migration/progenitor pathology.

evidence.snippet: Patient-derived organoids are significantly reduced in size, a change accompanied by a switch from symmetric to asymmetric cell division of ventricular zone radial glia cells (vRGCs).
evidence.explanation: Patient-specific MDS forebrain-type organoids link the reduced size to a symmetric-to-asymmetric division-mode switch in ventricular-zone radial glia, an upstream progenitor mechanism feeding the migration/cortical malformation; reinstating β-catenin signaling rescues the division modes.

steps/5.description: Disrupted nucleokinesis arrests migrating neurons before they reach their correct cortical layers during fetal corticogenesis. The result is a thickened, abnormally layered cortex with a smooth surface (agyria/ pachygyria), the defining classical (type I) lissencephaly of MDLS.

evidence.snippet: The most severe phenotype is Miller-Dieker syndrome (MDS) which is characterized by lissencephaly, dysmorphic facial features, growth failure, developmental disability, and often early death.
evidence.explanation: Identifies lissencephaly as a core defining feature of MDLS.

steps/6.description: Classical (type I) lissencephaly with agyria/pachygyria and an abnormally thick, smooth cortex.

evidence.snippet: Seizures occur in more than 90% of individuals with lissencephaly and often include infantile spasms.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents seizures in >90% of individuals with lissencephaly, supporting a VERY_FREQUENT classification.

steps/7.description: Epilepsy is highly frequent, often with onset in infancy and frequently including infantile spasms; seizures are often drug resistant.

evidence.snippet: Seizures occur in more than 90% of individuals with lissencephaly and often include infantile spasms.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists infantile spasms among the common seizure types.

steps/8.description: A characteristic early seizure type in PAFAH1B1-related lissencephaly.

evidence.snippet: even with good seizure control, the best developmental level achieved (excluding the few individuals with partial lissencephaly) is the equivalent of about age three to five months.
evidence.explanation: Supports a profound degree of developmental/intellectual impairment.

steps/9.description: Even with good seizure control, the best developmental level achieved is typically equivalent to age three to five months.

evidence.snippet: Other findings in PAFAH1B1-related lissencephaly/SBH include feeding issues and aspiration (which may result in need for gastrostomy tube placement), progressive microcephaly, and occasional developmental regression.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents progressive microcephaly as a feature.

steps/10.description: Progressive microcephaly is a documented feature of PAFAH1B1-related lissencephaly/SBH.

evidence.snippet: Affected newborns typically have mild-to-moderate hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and poor head control.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents neonatal hypotonia.

steps/11.description: Affected newborns typically have mild-to-moderate hypotonia; axial hypotonia is common and may coexist with distal spasticity.

evidence.snippet: mild distal spasticity that can transition over time to more severe spasticity.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents progressive spasticity.

steps/12.description: Mild distal spasticity early in life can transition over time to more severe spasticity.

evidence.snippet: Affected newborns typically have mild-to-moderate hypotonia, feeding difficulties, and poor head control.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents feeding difficulties from the neonatal period.

steps/13.description: Feeding difficulties and aspiration are common and may necessitate gastrostomy tube placement.

evidence.snippet: The most severe phenotype is Miller-Dieker syndrome (MDS) which is characterized by lissencephaly, dysmorphic facial features, growth failure, developmental disability, and often early death.
evidence.explanation: Lists growth failure among the defining features of MDLS.

steps/14.description: Growth failure is a recognized feature of the severe Miller-Dieker phenotype.

evidence.snippet: The most severe phenotype is Miller-Dieker syndrome (MDS) which is characterized by lissencephaly, dysmorphic facial features, growth failure, developmental disability, and often early death.
evidence.explanation: Lists dysmorphic facial features among the defining features of MDS specifically.

steps/15.description: Characteristic craniofacial dysmorphism is a defining feature of Miller-Dieker syndrome, classically including a prominent forehead, midface hypoplasia, small upturned nose, and thick upper lip (per the MONDO definition, NCIT:C124852).

evidence.snippet: in a fetus with lissencephaly, corpus callosum dysgenesis, ventriculomegaly, microcephaly, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), polyhydramnios and single umbilical artery.
evidence.explanation: Documents ventriculomegaly among the associated prenatal brain findings.

steps/16.description: Cerebral ventriculomegaly is a frequently associated brain finding, often detectable prenatally.

evidence.snippet: in a fetus with lissencephaly, corpus callosum dysgenesis, ventriculomegaly, microcephaly, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), polyhydramnios and single umbilical artery.
evidence.explanation: Documents corpus callosum dysgenesis among the associated brain malformations.

steps/17.description: Corpus callosum dysgenesis/agenesis can co-occur with the cortical malformation.

evidence.snippet: in a fetus with lissencephaly, corpus callosum dysgenesis, ventriculomegaly, microcephaly, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), polyhydramnios and single umbilical artery.
evidence.explanation: Documents IUGR as an associated prenatal finding.

steps/18.description: Prenatal growth restriction is commonly associated with the 17p13.3 deletion phenotype.

evidence.snippet: standard treatment for developmental delay/intellectual disability, spasticity, visual impairment, and hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists visual impairment among the manifestations requiring standard treatment, and recommends annual ophthalmologic evaluation.

steps/19.description: Affected individuals show poor visual tracking in the first years of life, and GeneReviews recommends standard treatment and annual ophthalmologic evaluation for visual impairment.

evidence.snippet: standard treatment for developmental delay/intellectual disability, spasticity, visual impairment, and hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists hearing loss among the manifestations requiring standard treatment, and recommends annual audiologic evaluation.

steps/20.description: Reduced response to sounds is noted on early neurologic examination, and GeneReviews recommends standard treatment and annual audiologic evaluation for hearing loss.

evidence.snippet: treatment with stool softeners, prokinetics, osmotic agents, or laxatives for constipation;
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents constipation as a recognized management concern requiring pharmacologic treatment and surveillance.

steps/21.description: Constipation is a recognized management concern, with GeneReviews recommending stool softeners, prokinetics, osmotic agents, or laxatives and surveillance for signs and symptoms of constipation.

evidence.snippet: Deletion of 17p13.3 has varying degrees of severity on brain development based on precise location and size of the deletion.
evidence.explanation: Supports the genotype-phenotype relationship in which deletion size and gene content determine severity.

evidence.snippet: We report a molecular cytogenetic characterization of 17p13.3 deletion syndrome by array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH), fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR)
evidence.explanation: Documents the molecular cytogenetic confirmation of a 17p13.3 deletion causing the syndrome.

genes/0.notes: The classical Miller-Dieker phenotype results from a 17p13.3 deletion that removes both PAFAH1B1 (LIS1) and YWHAE. PAFAH1B1 haploinsufficiency drives the lissencephaly, while co-deletion of YWHAE increases severity. Smaller deletions or intragenic PAFAH1B1 variants sparing YWHAE produce the milder isolated lissencephaly sequence.

evidence.snippet: we show that the gene encoding 14-3-3epsilon (YWHAE), one of a family of ubiquitous phosphoserine/threonine-binding proteins, is always deleted in individuals with MDS.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that YWHAE is consistently deleted in Miller-Dieker syndrome.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that deletion of 17p13.3 excluding PAFAH1B1 but including YWHAE is associated with a consistent phenotype and should be considered a distinct condition from MDS.
evidence.explanation: Clarifies that YWHAE-only deletions form a distinct, non-MDLS condition, delineating the genotype-phenotype boundary.

genes/1.notes: YWHAE encodes 14-3-3 epsilon. Its deletion is consistently present in Miller-Dieker syndrome and increases the severity of the migration defect relative to PAFAH1B1 loss alone. Deletions involving YWHAE but sparing PAFAH1B1 produce a distinct, milder condition rather than classical MDLS.

evidence.snippet: polytherapy with valproic acid and lamotrigine appears most effective in reducing drug-resistant seizures
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents the antiseizure regimen used in PAFAH1B1-related lissencephaly.

treatments/0.description: Management is centered on controlling seizures with antiseizure medications selected by seizure type; polytherapy with valproic acid and lamotrigine appears most effective in reducing drug-resistant seizures.

evidence.snippet: placement of a gastrostomy tube for those with failure to thrive, dysphagia, and/or recurrent aspiration pneumonia
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents gastrostomy tube placement for feeding and aspiration management.

treatments/1.description: Placement of a gastrostomy tube is used for individuals with failure to thrive, dysphagia, and/or recurrent aspiration pneumonia.

evidence.snippet: standard treatment for developmental delay/intellectual disability, spasticity, visual impairment, and hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents standard supportive treatment across the multisystem manifestations.

treatments/2.description: Standard supportive treatment for developmental delay/intellectual disability, spasticity, visual impairment, and hearing loss, with surveillance for nutrition, aspiration, and respiratory insufficiency.

evidence.snippet: Once the causative genetic alteration has been identified in the proband, prenatal testing may be offered to parents of an affected child because of the recurrence risk associated with the possibility of parental mosaicism or a balanced chromosome rearrangement.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents the genetic counseling and prenatal testing considerations.

treatments/3.description: Genetic counseling addresses recurrence risk, including the possibility of parental balanced rearrangement or germline mosaicism, and reproductive options such as prenatal testing.

open_questions/0.rationale: The dominant lissencephaly model — defective LIS1-dependent nucleokinesis/neuronal migration — derives largely from Pafah1b1 mutant mice and limited postmortem analysis. Because the mouse cortex is naturally lissencephalic and has few outer radial glia, it cannot test whether human-specific oRG progenitor biology contributes to MDS severity. Bershteyn et al. (PMID:28111201) found a prolonged-mitosis defect in oRG in MDS patient iPSC cerebral organoids, a progenitor subtype the authors note is "largely absent from lissencephalic rodents but critical for human neocortical expansion," and Iefremova et al. (PMID:28380362) found a non-cell-autonomous radial-glia division-mode switch. If oRG dysfunction is a genuine, human-enriched arm of MDS pathology, rodent models will systematically miss a progenitor-tier mechanism, which bears on how the migration vs. progenitor contributions to classical lissencephaly are weighted and modeled.

evidence.snippet: The first mutation disrupted the start codon and the second mutation resulted in an amino acid substitution.
evidence.explanation: Describes the index patient's two alleles, one of which abolishes translation initiation outright.

evidence.snippet: Two siblings from Family M harboured the homozygous missense variant c.1009C>T p.(R337C); this genotype has previously been reported in a patient with ataxia, hypotonia and developmental regression.
evidence.explanation: A further recessive genotype, and the observation that the same allele has been seen with a much broader phenotype.

evidence.snippet: p.G99 and p.R337 are in close proximity and involved in PPI interfaces with NDUFC1, NDUFC2 and ND2
evidence.explanation: In-silico structural modelling placing two NDUFA10 disease residues at interfaces with neighbouring subunits. Indirect: it locates the residues and does not measure what a substitution there does.

steps/1.description:
The initiating lesion. Reported alleles span the mutational spectrum a loss-of-function gene would be expected to show: a start-codon-destroying variant paired with a missense in the index patient, a homozygous missense in the second, and a homozygous in-frame single-residue deletion p.(A78del) plus a homozygous missense p.(R337C) in the optic-atrophy families.
Structural modelling in the 2026 series places two of these residues in the subunit's protein-protein interfaces rather than in any catalytic site, which is what an accessory-subunit lesion should look like: the variant degrades the subunit's ability to hold on to its neighbours, not its ability to turn over substrate.

evidence.snippet: NDUFA10 shares a deoxyribonucleoside kinase (dNK) domain with deoxyribonucleoside kinases in the nucleotide salvage pathway, though no specific function beyond stabilizing the complex I holoenzyme has been described for this subunit.
evidence.explanation: States the only established role of the subunit, which is what makes its loss a stability rather than a catalytic lesion.

evidence.snippet: This may be related to the role of accessory subunits, most of which are known to be necessary for human CI assembly and stability.
evidence.explanation: Places NDUFA10 in the class of accessory subunits required for assembly and stability. Indirect: a class-level statement, not a measurement on NDUFA10.

steps/2.description: The functional consequence common to every reported allele: complex I is built without a working copy of NDUFA10. What follows depends on what the subunit is for, and here the literature is unusually blunt - beyond stabilising the complex I holoenzyme, no specific function has been described for it. That is the ordinary reading of the disease, and the two hypothetical nodes below are the two candidate exceptions to it.

evidence.snippet: The fibroblasts of the patient displayed decreased amount and activity, and a disturbed assembly of complex I.
evidence.explanation: The assembly defect measured directly in patient-derived cells.

steps/3.description: Complex I assembly is disturbed in the patient's own fibroblasts. This is the step that distinguishes an accessory-subunit disease from a core-subunit one: a defective core subunit would be expected to leave a normal or near-normal amount of assembled enzyme with reduced turnover, whereas losing the scaffolding subunit costs the enzyme itself.

evidence.snippet: a vast majority of mitochondrial dGTP is tightly bound to NDUFA10, an accessory subunit of complex I of the mitochondrial respiratory chain
evidence.explanation: The measurement that makes NDUFA10 the mitochondrial dGTP reservoir.

evidence.snippet: This interaction may represent a hitherto unknown mechanism regulating mitochondrial dNTP availability and linking oxidative metabolism to DNA maintenance.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own framing of the consequence. Indirect, and hedged in the source itself - "may represent" - which is why this node is hypothetical.

steps/4.description:
A second property of NDUFA10 that has no counterpart in most complex I accessory subunits, and whose relevance to this disease is unknown. NDUFA10 retains a deoxyribonucleoside-kinase fold, and the large majority of the dGTP inside mitochondria is bound to it - tightly enough to survive mitochondrial isolation and methanol treatment. Engineering the dNK domain in HEK-293T cells, while deliberately preserving complex I assembly and activity, halves mitochondrial dGTP content. The authors propose the interaction as a link between oxidative metabolism and mitochondrial DNA maintenance.
Marked HYPOTHETICAL, and it is worth being precise about what is hypothetical. That NDUFA10 holds most mitochondrial dGTP is measured, not conjectured. What is conjectural is that this matters in MC1DN22: no patient allele has been tested for dGTP binding, no mitochondrial DNA depletion or deletion phenotype has been reported in an NDUFA10 patient, and the experiment that isolates the dGTP function used a mutant chosen precisely because it does *not* destabilise the complex - the opposite of what the disease alleles do. The node is curated because it is a testable prediction unique to this gene, not because there is evidence for it.

evidence.snippet: we found specific loss of phosphorylation of serine-250 in complex I subunit NdufA10
evidence.explanation: Identifies the regulated site. Indirect for this disease: the lesion under study is Pink1 loss in mouse, not an NDUFA10 variant in a patient.

evidence.snippet: Phosphorylation of serine-250 was needed for ubiquinone reduction by complex I.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the site gates quinone reduction, which is what would make its loss a functional rather than a structural deficit.

evidence.snippet: Here, the restoration of CI activity and partial rescue of locomotion does not appear to have a specific requirement for phosphorylation of ND42 at Ser-250.
evidence.explanation: Directly contradicts the serine-250 requirement in an independent fly system. It refutes the phospho-switch as the mechanism, not the broader finding that NDUFA10 abundance sets complex I activity - which the same study supports.

evidence.snippet: In Drosophila pink1 mutants, transgenic overexpression of ND42 or its co-chaperone sicily was sufficient to restore CI activity and partially rescue several phenotypes including flight and climbing deficits and mitochondrial disruption in flight muscles.
evidence.explanation: Supports the part both studies agree on: the amount of functional NDUFA10 is what sets complex I activity here. Split from the item above because one sentence supports the abundance claim while the other refutes the phospho-site claim.

steps/5.description:
A regulatory function of NDUFA10 discovered from the other end - not by studying NDUFA10 disease, but by asking why PINK1 loss reduces complex I activity. Phosphoproteomics of complex I in Pink1-null mouse liver and brain found a specific loss of phosphorylation at NdufA10 serine-250, and that phosphorylation turned out to be required for ubiquinone reduction by the complex.
The claim is contested, and the contradiction is curated below rather than smoothed over. An independent Drosophila study reached the opposite conclusion about the site itself: overexpressing ND42, the fly NDUFA10 homologue, did restore complex I activity and partially rescue locomotion in pink1 mutants, but that rescue showed no specific requirement for phosphorylation at Ser-250. So the two studies agree that NDUFA10 abundance governs complex I activity downstream of PINK1, and disagree about whether the serine-250 phospho-switch is the mechanism.
Whether any of this bears on MC1DN22 is a separate and unexamined question. No phosphorylation measurement has been made in an NDUFA10 patient's cells, and none of the alleles quotable here is described as affecting serine-250. The node is curated as a hypothesis about a second, potentially separable arm of the lesion, and its edge to the measured endpoint is typed as having unknown intermediates for that reason.

evidence.snippet: The fibroblasts of the patient displayed decreased amount and activity, and a disturbed assembly of complex I.
evidence.explanation: Measures both the quantity and the function of the enzyme in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: We report a patient with Leigh syndrome who showed a complex I deficiency expressed in cultured fibroblasts and muscle tissue.
evidence.explanation: Shows the deficiency is expressed in an affected tissue as well as in cultured cells, which is what makes it more than a fibroblast artefact.

steps/6.description:
The measured endpoint, and the best-evidenced claim in this entry. Both the amount and the activity of complex I fall, in fibroblasts and in muscle tissue, and the two falling together is the signature of an assembly or stability defect rather than a catalytic one.
Conformance note: the module pairs decreased oxidative phosphorylation with increased reactive oxygen species. Only the first arm is evidenced here - reactive oxygen species have not been measured in an NDUFA10 patient and are not asserted. The module's upstream node, age-related mitochondrial damage and mtDNA mutation, does not apply to a primary nuclear subunit defect, so conformance is declared at this node alone.

evidence.snippet: LS is pathologically uniformly characterized by multifocal bilateral and symmetric spongiform degeneration of the basal ganglia, brainstem, thalamus, cerebellum, spinal cord, and optic nerves.
evidence.explanation: Gives the lesion distribution this node names. Indirect for MC1DN22: it describes Leigh syndrome as an entity, not this patient's neuropathology.

evidence.snippet: Isolated complex I deficiency is the most common defect identified in Leigh syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Connects the biochemical lesion of this entry to the syndrome, at class level.

steps/7.description:
The severe pole. Leigh syndrome is a pathological diagnosis as much as a clinical one - bilateral, symmetric spongiform degeneration of the basal ganglia, brainstem, thalamus, cerebellum, spinal cord and optic nerves - and isolated complex I deficiency is its commonest biochemical cause. Two NDUFA10 patients have carried that diagnosis, and the gene appears among the nuclear Leigh genes of a 219-patient Russian cohort.
Marked PROVISIONAL rather than ESTABLISHED because the association between NDUFA10 loss and this lesion distribution rests on a small number of patients diagnosed clinically and radiologically; no NDUFA10 case has been examined neuropathologically, and why complex I deficiency selects these structures is not answered by any source cited here. The edge into this node is typed with unknown intermediates for the same reason: the steps between a cell-level bioenergetic deficit and a stereotyped lesion distribution are exactly what is missing.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, isolated or plus OA was found for the first time in NDUFV2, NDUFA1, NDUFA10 and NDUFAF3 families, for which only a single report of arLHON existed for a patient carrying NDUFA10 variants.
evidence.explanation: Establishes optic atrophy as a presentation of biallelic NDUFA10 variants.

steps/8.description:
The mild pole, and the reason this entity is not simply "NDUFA10 Leigh syndrome". A 2026 screen of complex I genes in patients with optic atrophy found biallelic NDUFA10 variants in three families and reported optic atrophy - isolated in one of them - as a presentation of this gene for the first time. The optic nerve is not a surprising target: it is already on the list of structures degenerating in Leigh syndrome, and retinal ganglion cells are the classic casualty of complex I failure in the mitochondrial optic neuropathies.
PROVISIONAL because the number of families is small, because the series is a targeted ascertainment of patients who already had optic atrophy - so it cannot say how often NDUFA10 disease presents this way - and because no mechanism specific to retinal ganglion cells has been demonstrated for this gene.

evidence.snippet: We report a patient with Leigh syndrome who showed a complex I deficiency expressed in cultured fibroblasts and muscle tissue.
evidence.explanation: Documents the complex I deficiency in the index patient, in two tissues.

steps/9.description: The defining biochemical phenotype, and the finding that brings a patient to NDUFA10 sequencing in the first place. In the index case it was demonstrated in cultured fibroblasts and in muscle, alongside a reduced amount of the complex and a disturbed assembly.

evidence.snippet: We report a patient with Leigh syndrome who showed a complex I deficiency expressed in cultured fibroblasts and muscle tissue.
evidence.explanation: The diagnosis in the index patient.

evidence.snippet: Here, we present an additional description of a child with Leigh syndrome harboring a homozygous mutation in NDUFA10, providing insights in clinical, biochemical, and neuroradiologic features for future earlier recognition.
evidence.explanation: The diagnosis in the second reported patient.

evidence.snippet: Using massive parallel sequencing we were able to detect pathogenic variants in other 16 LS nuclear genes: NDUFV1, NDUFS2, NDUFS8, NDUFAF5, NDUFAF6, NDUFA10, SUCLG1, GFM2, COX10, PMPCB, NARS2, PDHB, SLC19A3 and IARS2
evidence.explanation: NDUFA10 among the nuclear genes solved in a national Leigh cohort. Indirect: the sentence names the gene in a list and does not say how many of the 219 patients carried it or what they looked like.

steps/10.description:
Curated as a clinical diagnosis rather than decomposed into HPO signs, because that is the granularity at which the sources report it. HPO has no term for Leigh syndrome - it is a disease concept, held in MONDO and OMIM - so `phenotype_term` carries a free-text `preferred_term` with no binding, rather than a substituted approximation such as an abnormal-basal-ganglia term, which would assert an imaging finding not reported per patient here.
Two patients carry the diagnosis in the primary reports, and NDUFA10 also appears among the nuclear genes solved in a 219-patient Russian Leigh cohort - a third, unquantified ascertainment.
A published third case exists and is not curated as evidence. PMID:36270260 is a letter titled "Juvenile-onset dystonia with spasticity in Leigh syndrome caused by a novel NDUFA10 variant"; it has no abstract, and neither PubMed nor its DOI returns any body text, so its cached record is empty. Its title is the only accessible statement about it, and a title is not a finding. Dystonia and spasticity are therefore NOT curated as phenotypes of this entity, and the juvenile onset it reports is not curated either.

evidence.snippet: we observed isolated OA in two siblings homozygous for the NDUFA10 p.(R337C) variant, whereas a previously published case with the same amino acid change was reported to have multisystemic involvement.
evidence.explanation: Isolated optic atrophy in two NDUFA10 patients, together with the intra-allelic discordance that is the striking part of the observation.

evidence.snippet: In all patients, OA began during childhood, except for Family N, which exhibited a LHON-like onset.
evidence.explanation: The onset pattern in the accessory-subunit families. Indirect and hedged: the sentence covers Families H-O across four genes, and Family N is not an NDUFA10 family, so it constrains rather than specifies the NDUFA10 tempo.

steps/11.description: The presentation of the 2026 cohort, and in two siblings the entire disease. Recorded without a frequency band on purpose: the cohort was ascertained by starting from patients who already had optic atrophy, so its share of NDUFA10 patients tells you about the screen's design rather than about the disease. What the same series does establish is a genuine phenotypic discordance within a single allele - two siblings homozygous for p.(R337C) had isolated optic atrophy, while a previously published patient with the same amino-acid change had multisystem disease.

evidence.snippet: Two siblings from Family M harboured the homozygous missense variant c.1009C>T p.(R337C); this genotype has previously been reported in a patient with ataxia, hypotonia and developmental regression.
evidence.explanation: Ataxia in an NDUFA10 patient. Indirect because the 2026 authors are reporting another group's case rather than their own examination.

steps/12.description: Reported in the previously published patient homozygous for NDUFA10 p.(R337C), described in the 2026 series as having had multisystem involvement - the same allele that gave two siblings isolated optic atrophy. Recorded without a frequency band: this is one patient, reached second-hand through a citation in the 2026 paper.

evidence.snippet: Two siblings from Family M harboured the homozygous missense variant c.1009C>T p.(R337C); this genotype has previously been reported in a patient with ataxia, hypotonia and developmental regression.
evidence.explanation: Hypotonia in an NDUFA10 patient, reported second-hand in the 2026 series.

steps/13.description: Reported in the same previously published NDUFA10 p.(R337C) patient. One patient, second-hand; no frequency band.

evidence.snippet: Two siblings from Family M harboured the homozygous missense variant c.1009C>T p.(R337C); this genotype has previously been reported in a patient with ataxia, hypotonia and developmental regression.
evidence.explanation: Developmental regression in an NDUFA10 patient, reported second-hand in the 2026 series.

steps/14.description: Reported in the same previously published NDUFA10 p.(R337C) patient. Regression - loss of skills already acquired - is the tempo that separates a mitochondrial encephalopathy from a static developmental disorder, which is why it is curated separately from the Leigh diagnosis rather than folded into it. One patient, second-hand; no frequency band.

evidence.snippet: Cerebellar atrophy was reported in two cases (Family J and L).
evidence.explanation: Cerebellar atrophy in Family L, which the same paper identifies as one of the two families homozygous for the NDUFA10 in-frame deletion p.(A78del). Indirect because the sentence names families rather than genes, so the gene attribution comes from the paper's genotype passage rather than from this sentence alone; Family J is an NDUFA1 family and is not claimed here.

steps/15.description:
Reported in one of the two NDUFA10 families in the 2026 optic-atrophy series. The attribution needs its reasoning stated, because the quoted sentence names two families without naming their genes: cerebellar atrophy was found in Families J and L, and the same paper assigns Family J to NDUFA1 and Families K and L to the homozygous NDUFA10 p.(A78del) allele. So Family L is the NDUFA10 case and Family J is not. That is a structural inference across two passages of one paper rather than a single quotable statement, which is why the evidence below is marked INDIRECT and why the reasoning is written out here rather than left for the reader to reconstruct.
One patient, so no frequency band. It is worth curating because it is the only structural neuroimaging finding attributed to an NDUFA10 patient anywhere in the citable literature, and because cerebellar atrophy sits outside the optic nerve - evidence that even the mild pole of this entity is not always confined to the visual pathway.

edges/3.description: Typed with unknown intermediates because whether a disease allele actually abolishes dGTP binding has never been tested; the engineered dNK-domain mutant that does abolish it is a different, deliberately assembly-sparing change.

edges/4.description: Typed with unknown intermediates because the serine-250 result comes from Pink1-null mouse tissue, and no NDUFA10 patient allele has been examined for an effect on this site.

evidence.snippet: We identified compound-heterozygous mutations in the NDUFA10 gene, encoding an accessory subunit of complex I.
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease assignment that defines the entity.

evidence.snippet: The proband from Families K and L carried the homozygous in-frame deletion c.233_235del p.(A78del).
evidence.explanation: A recurrent NDUFA10 allele across two families in the optic-atrophy cohort.

genes/0.notes:
NDUFA10 encodes the NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase subunit A10, an accessory subunit of the complex I membrane arm. Reading the literature on this gene needs one caution: most NDUFA10 papers are not about this disease. The gene appears constantly as a member of expression signatures in cancer transcriptomics, in Parkinson-disease models through its PINK1 connection, and in cardiac ischaemia-reperfusion work. The disease literature is four reports.
A second caution concerns the alleles themselves. Both a start-codon variant and single-residue missense and in-frame-deletion changes have been reported, and there is no evident hotspot - the residues modelled in the 2026 series sit at interfaces with NDUFC1, NDUFC2 and ND2 rather than in a single domain. Three specific alleles are quotable and are cited on the evidence items here: the compound-heterozygous pair in the index case, described only as a start-codon disruption plus a substitution; the homozygous in-frame deletion c.233_235del p.(A78del) in two optic-atrophy families; and the homozygous c.1009C>T p.(R337C) in a third, which had already been reported in a patient with a much broader phenotype.
Uncited leads, from the deep-research report committed with this entry, which had full-text access to the two paywalled case reports. The index patient's alleles are given there as c.1A>G (start-loss, p.Met1?) inherited from the father and c.425A>G (p.Gln142Arg) from the mother, both absent from 108 controls and from 21 further patients with isolated complex I deficiency. The 2017 patient is given as homozygous c.296G>A (p.Gly99Glu), with heterozygous third-degree-cousin parents. Neither is curated as evidence: the cached record for both papers is abstract-only, and neither abstract names an allele.
One discrepancy for the next curator to resolve rather than inherit. The 2026 series states that p.(A78del) had previously been reported *in trans* with p.(G99E) in a case of Leigh syndrome, while the deep-research report gives the 2017 patient as a p.(G99E) homozygote. Those cannot both describe the same patient. Either a third G99E case exists, or one of the two descriptions is wrong; nothing quotable here settles it, and no phase claim is made in this entry as a result.

open_questions/0.rationale:
This is the sharpest open question in the entity, and it is sharper than the usual mitochondrial-disease variability complaint because the genotype is held constant: the same amino-acid change, homozygous, on both sides of the comparison. Whatever separates the two poles of MC1DN22 is therefore not the allele.
The 2026 authors offer the standard candidates - nuclear and mitochondrial modifiers, environmental exposure - and note that some of their patients carried mitochondrial-DNA variants of uncertain effect that might act synergistically or antagonistically with the nuclear lesion. None of this is demonstrated for NDUFA10.
Closing the gap needs residual complex I amount and activity measured in both kinds of patient with the same assay, which has not been done: the biochemical work in this entity is fifteen years old and comes from the severe pole only.

open_questions/1.rationale:
Curated as HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH rather than KNOWLEDGE_GAP because the evidence is not missing. Both functions are well demonstrated - the dGTP reservoir in mouse tissue and human HEK-293T cells, the serine-250 switch in Pink1-null mouse liver and brain, in Drosophila and in cells from PINK1 patients. What is untested is their relationship to a patient carrying an NDUFA10 variant.
The mismatch has a specific shape in each case, and the shapes are different. For dGTP, the experiment that isolated the function used an engineered dNK-domain mutant chosen because it preserves complex I assembly and activity - the opposite of the disease alleles, which destabilise the complex. So the cleanest demonstration of the dGTP function is also the one least like the disease. For serine-250, the lesion studied was Pink1 loss, not an NDUFA10 variant; NDUFA10 appears there as the substrate through which a different disease acts.
The practical consequence is a prediction nobody has checked: if the dGTP reservoir matters, NDUFA10 patients might show mitochondrial DNA copy-number or integrity abnormalities that other complex I subunit deficiencies do not. No such measurement has been reported.

evidence.snippet: We report the first missense mutation within the nuclear encoded complex I subunit, NDUFS7, in 2 siblings with neuropathologically proven complex I-deficient Leigh syndrome.
evidence.explanation: The founding report establishing NDUFS7 as a disease gene.

evidence.snippet: While homozygosity for a V122M substitution in NDUFS7 (PSST) has been found in two siblings with neuropathologically proven Leigh syndrome
evidence.explanation: Names the founding allele and its homozygous state, which the 1999 abstract itself does not spell out.

evidence.snippet: The homozygous mutation at nucleotide (nt) 434 G>A resulted in the modification of the arginine 145 to histidine in a highly conserved region of the protein.
evidence.explanation: The second reported allele, with the conservation argument for its pathogenicity.

evidence.snippet: The mutation was absent from over than 100 healthy controls from the same ethnic origin.
evidence.explanation: The control-population evidence that separates a causal allele from an ancestry-specific polymorphism.

evidence.snippet: This mutation lies in the first intron of the NDUFS7 gene (c.17-1167 C>G) and creates a strong donor splice site resulting in the generation of a cryptic exon.
evidence.explanation: The splice-altering allele class, which is why a coding-only analysis can miss this gene.

evidence.snippet: This mutation is predicted to result in a shortened mutant protein of 41 instead of 213 amino acids containing only the first five amino acids of the normal protein.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies how little protein survives the splice allele - effectively a null.

evidence.snippet: This study shows that the NDUFS7 c.16 + 5G > A variant (rs375282422) has a causative role in Leigh syndrome.
evidence.explanation: A second, independent splice-region allele, recorded with its dbSNP identifier.

steps/1.description:
Biallelic NDUFS7 variants. The reported alleles fall into two mechanistic classes, and the distinction matters downstream.
Missense alleles leave a protein to be made: V122M, homozygous in the 1999 sibling pair and the first missense mutation found in any nuclear-encoded complex I subunit; R145H, homozygous in a consanguineous family, altering a highly conserved region and absent from over a hundred ethnically matched controls; and the further L126F and R168S alleles that later structural work grouped with them.
Splice alleles remove the protein instead. A first-intron variant (c.17-1167C>G) creates a strong donor splice site and a cryptic exon, predicted to yield a 41-residue product retaining only the first five amino acids of the normal 213; the intronic c.16+5G>A variant found in Finnish siblings likewise acts through splicing.
Note on nomenclature: the founding allele is written V122M in the yeast reconstruction and V112M in the fibroblast panel that used the same cell line. That is a numbering difference, not two alleles, and a curator matching variant strings across these papers should expect it.

evidence.snippet: The quinone headgroup binds at the deep end of this chamber, near iron-sulphur cluster N2.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the spatial relationship between the quinone site and cluster N2 that makes the Q module the terminal electron-transfer step.

evidence.snippet: NADH transfers two electrons to FMN as a hydride ion and then electrons are transferred one by one, along the uniquely long (95 Å) chain of seven conserved Fe-S clusters, to the quinone-binding site at the interface with the membrane domain.
evidence.explanation: Gives the whole electron path, whose final step the Q-module lesion interrupts.

evidence.snippet: the subunit most frequently affected in our OA cohort, which is located at the junction between the peripheral and membrane arms of CI and is involved in the formation of the CoQ binding site
evidence.explanation: Locates NDUFS7 specifically, in the words of the study that mapped its variants onto the human complex I structure.

evidence.snippet: The data show a drastic decrease in Q reductase activity upon mutating several residues despite full assembly of the complex.
evidence.explanation: The experiment that separates the catalytic lesion from the assembly lesion. Full assembly, no activity, from PSST loop residues alone.

evidence.snippet: revealed remarkable ejection of the bound Q from the site near terminal electron donor N2
evidence.explanation: The proposed physical mechanism, from molecular dynamics rather than measurement, which is why it is graded COMPUTATIONAL and separately from the assay result above.

steps/2.description:
What NDUFS7/PSST actually does, and the reason a missense allele here is not equivalent to losing an accessory subunit. Complex I transfers two electrons from NADH to FMN and then one at a time along a ninety-five-angstrom chain of seven conserved iron-sulfur clusters to a quinone-binding site at the interface with the membrane domain. That site is unusually long, narrow and enclosed, and the quinone headgroup binds at its deep end, immediately adjacent to cluster N2 - the cluster that donates the electrons. NDUFS7 sits at the junction between the peripheral and membrane arms and contributes to forming that site.
The functional consequence has been isolated experimentally. Mutating conserved residues in the PSST loop that faces the roughly thirty-angstrom Q-binding tunnel causes a drastic decrease in quinone reductase activity despite full assembly of the complex, and molecular dynamics of the arginine variants shows the bound quinone being ejected from the site near N2. This is a catalytic lesion, separable from the assembly lesion that the truncating alleles produce.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of the assembly state of the respiratory chain complexes under native condition revealed a marked decrease of fully assembled complex I while the quantity of the other complexes was not altered.
evidence.explanation: The direct measurement of the assembly defect, together with the isolation of that defect to complex I alone.

evidence.snippet: This study demonstrates clinical, neuroradiological, and molecular genetic findings in siblings with Leigh syndrome and isolated complex I assembly defect associated with intronic c.16 + 5G > A variant in the NDUFS7 gene.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication of an isolated assembly defect from a second splice allele.

evidence.snippet: NDUFAF8 contributes to early stabilization of NDUFS7 together with NDUFAF5
evidence.explanation: Places NDUFS7 at an early, chaperone-dependent step of Q-module assembly. Graded OTHER because the sentence summarises published complexome profiling rather than reporting this study's own experiment.

evidence.snippet: BN-PAGE revealed no such association in LS patient fibroblasts with mutations in other CI subunit-encoding genes where NDUFAF2 was attached to CI-830 (NDUFS1, NDUFV1 mutation) or not detected (NDUFS7 mutation)
evidence.explanation: Records the NDUFS7-specific negative - NDUFAF2 absent from complex I in these cells, unlike the other subunit mutants tested in the same experiment.

steps/3.description:
The second, separable arm of the lesion. Native analysis of respiratory-chain complexes in the cryptic-exon patient showed a marked decrease of fully assembled complex I while the other complexes were unaltered - the definition of an isolated, assembly-level complex I defect. The Finnish siblings with the c.16+5G>A allele were likewise characterised as having an isolated complex I assembly defect on blue native PAGE.
NDUFS7 enters the assembly pathway early: complexome profiling places NDUFAF8, together with NDUFAF5, at the early stabilisation of NDUFS7, which is why a defect in this subunit stalls Q-module maturation rather than removing a late decorative step.
A negative observation from an unrelated study is worth recording here because it is specific to this gene: in patient fibroblasts carrying an NDUFS7 mutation, the assembly factor NDUFAF2 was not detected on complex I at all, whereas in NDUFS1- and NDUFV1-mutant cells it remained attached to the 830-kDa subcomplex. Whatever intermediate NDUFAF2 normally holds is not formed or not retained when NDUFS7 is defective.

evidence.snippet: Mitochondrial membranes from Y. lipolytica strains carrying any of the three point mutations exhibited similar complex I defects, with V(max) being reduced by about 50%.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the catalytic consequence of the patient allele in a reconstituted enzyme, where nothing else about the cell differs.

evidence.snippet: In addition changes in the K(m) for n-decyl-ubiquinone and I(50) for hydrophobic complex I inhibitors were observed, which provides further evidence that not only the hydrophobic, mitochondrially coded subunits, but also some of the nuclear coded subunits of complex I are involved in its reaction with ubiquinone.
evidence.explanation: Two independent quinone-site readouts change, which is what localises the defect to the reaction with ubiquinone rather than to enzyme quantity.

evidence.snippet: For control cells, the ratio between activity and amount was 1 whereas for the patients this ratio was below 1, indicating a defect in intrinsic catalytic activity of complex I in the latter cells.
evidence.explanation: In a fibroblast panel that includes an NDUFS7 patient line, separates the quantity defect from the quality defect and shows both are present.

steps/4.description:
The measured biochemical endpoint: reduced NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase activity, with the rest of the respiratory chain intact. Reconstructing the patient V122M substitution in the homologous subunit of Yarrowia lipolytica halves Vmax, and the same experiment records altered Km for n-decyl-ubiquinone and altered I50 for hydrophobic complex I inhibitors - both quinone-site readouts. The authors take this as evidence that nuclear-coded subunits, not only the hydrophobic mitochondrially coded ones, participate in the reaction with ubiquinone, which is precisely the claim the upstream Q-module node makes structurally.
The fibroblast panel that includes an NDUFS7 line adds the amount-versus-activity decomposition: in controls the ratio of complex I activity to complex I amount is one, and in patients it is below one, so the enzyme that does assemble is intrinsically less catalytically competent. The deficiency is quantitative and qualitative at once, which is what a core Q-module subunit defect predicts.

evidence.snippet: Patient cells displayed increased ROS levels and a variable decrease in complex I activity and amount.
evidence.explanation: Both arms of the module node measured together in a panel that includes an NDUFS7 patient line.

evidence.snippet: the absence of NDUFS7 resulted in reduced cell proliferation, elevated cell death, and increased susceptibility to oxidative stress
evidence.explanation: An NDUFS7-specific cellular model tying loss of the subunit directly to oxidative vulnerability and death.

evidence.snippet: Cell models of mitochondrial complex I (CI) deficiency display activation of glycolysis to compensate for the loss in mitochondrial ATP production. This adaptation can mask other relevant deficiency-induced aberrations in cell physiology.
evidence.explanation: The glycolytic compensation that conceals the bioenergetic deficit in culture, and the reason the galactose protocol is needed to see it.

evidence.snippet: Following optimization of the cell culture protocol, LS fibroblasts died in the galactose medium, whereas control cells did not.
evidence.explanation: Removing the glycolytic escape route unmasks a lethal deficit in patient cells specifically, including the NDUFS7 line in this panel.

steps/5.description:
Cellular oxidative phosphorylation capacity falls and reactive oxygen species rise. Both arms of the module node are evidenced here rather than only one: an NDUFS7-containing fibroblast panel shows raised ROS alongside reduced complex I activity and amount, and an engineered NDUFS7 mutation in HEK293T cells produces reduced proliferation, elevated cell death and increased susceptibility to oxidative stress.
Two caveats a curator should carry forward. First, cultured cells hide the deficit: complex I-deficient cells upregulate glycolysis to replace the lost mitochondrial ATP, and that adaptation masks other consequences - which is why the NDUFS7 line only dies when glucose is replaced by galactose in a pyruvate-free medium. The clinical counterpart is decompensation under catabolic stress. Second, the cells are not defenceless: upregulated SLC7A11 imports cystine and raises glutathione, and that response measurably limits the cell death caused by NDUFS7 deficiency.
Conformance note: the module's upstream node - age-related mitochondrial damage and mtDNA mutation - does not apply to a primary nuclear-gene subunit defect, so conformance is declared at this node alone.

evidence.snippet: in 2 siblings with neuropathologically proven complex I-deficient Leigh syndrome
evidence.explanation: Neuropathological rather than radiological confirmation in the founding cases, which is the strongest form this observation takes.

evidence.snippet: Brain MRI showed characteristic bilateral symmetrical T2 hyperintense lesions, histologically representing encephalomalacia.
evidence.explanation: Ties the imaging appearance to its histological substrate in an NDUFS7-mutant animal, which is not obtainable from the human cases.

steps/6.description: Selective failure of the basal ganglia, midbrain and brainstem, producing the bilateral symmetrical T2-hyperintense lesions that define Leigh syndrome. It is the anatomical signature of this entity: the founding siblings had neuropathologically proven Leigh syndrome, the Finnish siblings showed early basal ganglia and midbrain involvement, and the canine model reproduces both the imaging pattern and the underlying encephalomalacia.

evidence.snippet: The variants in the CI core subunits (NDUFS7, NDUFV1 and NDUFV2) were associated with isolated OA in six of eight patients
evidence.explanation: The core-subunit optic-atrophy result, of which NDUFS7 was the largest component.

evidence.snippet: The homozygous variant c.313C>T p.(R105C) was found in affected individuals from Families D and E, making NDUFS7 the most commonly affected gene in our case series.
evidence.explanation: Recurrence of the same homozygous allele in two unrelated families, which is the independent-observation argument for this association.

evidence.snippet: These patients typically exhibited isolated OA, with either an insidious onset during childhood or an acute/subacute onset similar to LHON in young adulthood
evidence.explanation: Characterises the temporal course, which is the feature that makes this presentation reach an ophthalmologist rather than a metabolic clinic.

steps/7.description:
The other end of the tissue spectrum, and the newer of the two. In a 2026 optic-neuropathy cohort NDUFS7 was the most frequently affected gene, and biallelic core-subunit variants produced isolated optic atrophy in six of eight patients, with either insidious childhood onset or an acute to subacute young-adult course indistinguishable from Leber hereditary optic neuropathy. NDUFS7 is among the genes that series associates with the autosomal recessive LHON phenotype.
Curated PROVISIONAL for the tissue claim specifically: the association rests on one large case series with in-silico rather than functional validation of the new alleles, and none of the classical Leigh-associated NDUFS7 patients was reported with isolated optic involvement. The mechanistic proposal for why the same gene should do two different things is curated separately as a hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: We report the first missense mutation within the nuclear encoded complex I subunit, NDUFS7, in 2 siblings with neuropathologically proven complex I-deficient Leigh syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Neuropathologically proven Leigh syndrome in the founding NDUFS7 patients.

evidence.snippet: findings in siblings with Leigh syndrome and isolated complex I assembly defect associated with intronic c.16 + 5G > A variant in the NDUFS7 gene
evidence.explanation: An independent NDUFS7 sibling pair with the same clinical diagnosis, two decades after the founding report.

steps/8.description: Subacute necrotising encephalomyelopathy with bilateral symmetrical basal ganglia and brainstem lesions. It is the defining presentation of this entity and was neuropathologically proven in the founding sibling pair; the more recent Finnish siblings show early basal ganglia and midbrain involvement on imaging.

evidence.snippet: Patients show developmental regression, dystonia, ataxia, and dysphagia.
evidence.explanation: Names developmental regression among the defining features of the Leigh syndrome spectrum. Graded OTHER because the sentence is definitional Leigh-spectrum background in the introduction of a canine/Drosophila study that reports no human data of its own - not an NDUFS7 patient-level observation.

steps/9.description:
Loss of previously acquired motor and cognitive milestones, the feature that distinguishes the Leigh syndrome course from a static encephalopathy.
Scope caveat: the evidence here is a general statement about Leigh syndrome patients in the introduction of the canine study, not an itemised observation in a genotyped human NDUFS7 patient. It is curated because regression is intrinsic to the Leigh diagnosis those patients carry, but the reader should know the citation is definitional.

evidence.snippet: The dogs presented with progressive ataxia, dystonia, and increased lactate levels.
evidence.explanation: Dystonia observed directly in animals homozygous for an NDUFS7 missense variant.

evidence.snippet: Patients show developmental regression, dystonia, ataxia, and dysphagia.
evidence.explanation: The human background for the canine observation above: dystonia is named among the defining features of the Leigh syndrome spectrum. Graded OTHER because it is definitional Leigh-spectrum background from the introduction of a canine/Drosophila study, not an NDUFS7 patient-level observation.

steps/10.description: Dystonic movement disorder, the expected consequence of symmetrical basal ganglia injury. Documented directly in the NDUFS7-mutant dogs and named among the defining features of the human Leigh syndrome spectrum.

evidence.snippet: The variants in the CI core subunits (NDUFS7, NDUFV1 and NDUFV2) were associated with isolated OA in six of eight patients
evidence.explanation: The core-subunit optic-atrophy finding, of which NDUFS7 was the most frequently affected gene.

evidence.snippet: In 12 cases, the subacute onset of vision loss enabled us to associate or confirm novel genes (NDUFS7, NDUFV1, NDUFAF2, NDUFAF4, NDUFAF8) with the autosomal recessive Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (arLHON) phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Names NDUFS7 among the genes associated with the recessive LHON phenotype, which is the specific clinical shape of this presentation.

steps/11.description: Bilateral optic nerve atrophy which, in the 2026 series, was the only manifestation in most core-subunit patients, presenting either insidiously in childhood or acutely in young adulthood in the manner of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy. This substantially widens the clinical differential in which NDUFS7 belongs: an adult with subacute bilateral vision loss and no mtDNA LHON mutation is a candidate for biallelic NDUFS7 variants.

edges/1.description: A defective or absent core Q-module subunit compromises the structure that carries cluster N2 and forms the quinone site.

evidence.snippet: These results report the first intronic NDUFS7 gene mutation and demonstrate the crucial role of NDUFS7 in the biogenesis of complex I.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own statement of the causal step from the gene defect to a biogenesis failure.

edges/2.description: Truncating and splice alleles remove the subunit, and the holoenzyme cannot be assembled or maintained without it.

edges/3.description: A compromised quinone site adjacent to the terminal cluster is a compromised final electron-transfer step.

edges/4.description: Less assembled enzyme means less NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase capacity, independently of any catalytic defect in the enzyme that does assemble.

edges/5.description: Reduced electron flux into the ubiquinone pool lowers proton pumping and oxidative phosphorylation capacity.

edges/6.description: The most oxidative-phosphorylation-dependent grey matter fails first.

edges/7.description: The retinal ganglion cells and their axons are the other classically energy-limited target of complex I disease.

evidence.snippet: We report the first missense mutation within the nuclear encoded complex I subunit, NDUFS7, in 2 siblings with neuropathologically proven complex I-deficient Leigh syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the gene-disease relationship.

evidence.snippet: The homozygous mutation at nucleotide (nt) 434 G>A resulted in the modification of the arginine 145 to histidine in a highly conserved region of the protein.
evidence.explanation: An independent family and allele, confirming the relationship.

evidence.snippet: The homozygous variant c.313C>T p.(R105C) was found in affected individuals from Families D and E, making NDUFS7 the most commonly affected gene in our case series.
evidence.explanation: Two further unrelated families sharing a homozygous allele, extending the gene's phenotypic range to isolated optic atrophy.

genes/0.notes: NDUFS7 encodes PSST, a nuclear-encoded core subunit of the complex I Q module. Reported disease alleles are homozygous in every well-characterised pedigree and fall into a missense class (V122M, R145H, L126F, R168S, and the optic-atrophy alleles R75C, R100C, R105C) and a splice class (c.17-1167C>G generating a cryptic exon, and c.16+5G>A). Inheritance is autosomal recessive throughout and is recorded in the entry's `inheritance` block.

evidence.snippet: Pharmacological treatments for OA included idebenone, CoQ10, riboflavin and ubidecarenone at variable dosages. Visual improvement was variable, with only 3 of 13 patients showing some degree of response to idebenone treatment
evidence.explanation: Supports that these agents are used in practice, and records the minority response rate that goes with them. It is an uncontrolled series spanning several genes, so it does not establish efficacy in NDUFS7 disease.

treatments/0.description: Idebenone, coenzyme Q10, riboflavin and ubidecarenone were given at variable doses to patients in the optic-atrophy series. Curated with its outcome attached, which is the reason it is worth curating at all: visual improvement was variable and only three of thirteen patients showed any degree of response to idebenone. That is a real but small effect in a small, uncontrolled, genetically mixed series, and it should not be read as evidence that idebenone works in NDUFS7 disease specifically.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Short-chain quinone analogues are given on the rationale that they can shuttle electrons into complex III and bypass a defective complex I, which is the step this entity's lesion blocks. The rationale is mechanistic; the clinical result recorded below is equivocal.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, in the NDUFS7 subunit, partial spatial segregation was observed for missense variants associated with either Leigh syndrome or isolated optic atrophy, suggesting possible disease-specific molecular defects.
evidence.explanation: The hypothesis as its authors state it, with their hedges - partial, possible - intact.

evidence.snippet: the former were grouped close to the Fe-S cluster N2, associated with the ubiquinone (coenzyme Q10, CoQ10) binding site, while the latter were situated in the N-terminal of the subunit
evidence.explanation: The structural observation the hypothesis rests on - two spatially distinct variant groups within one subunit.

evidence.snippet: Among these variants, p.(L126F), p.(R145H) and p.(R168S), associated with LS, were also predicted to have an impact on protein folding based on their ΔΔG values.
evidence.explanation: Names the Leigh-associated alleles and records that the pathogenicity argument for them is predictive, not experimental.

hypotheses/0.description:
The proposal is that the two clinical poles of NDUFS7 disease are not modifier-driven but position-driven within a single subunit. Variants associated with Leigh syndrome - L126F, R145H, R168S - cluster close to iron-sulfur cluster N2 and the coenzyme Q binding site, where they should impair the terminal electron-transfer step directly. Variants found in isolated optic atrophy - R75C, R100C, R105C - sit instead in the N-terminal region of the subunit, peripherally, where they mediate protein-protein interfaces with NDUFS2, NDUFS8, NDUFA7 and NDUFA12 rather than lining the catalytic site.
If this holds, the same gene produces a severe infantile encephalopathy or an adult-onset optic neuropathy according to whether the lesion is catalytic or interfacial, and the structural position of a novel allele becomes prognostically informative. It is graded EMERGING because the segregation is explicitly described as partial, rests on one cohort mapped onto a single structure, and is supported by in-silico prediction rather than functional assays of the new alleles. ND1 is noted as the one interaction partner shared across both variant groups, which is a caveat rather than a refutation.

open_questions/0.rationale: The spatial segregation of the two variant groups is a structural observation supported by folding predictions, not by enzymology. Nobody has yet measured complex I assembly and activity side by side in cells carrying an N-terminal allele and a cluster-N2-adjacent allele. Until that is done, the position-determines-phenotype hypothesis remains a plausible reading of a variant map. The Yarrowia reconstruction and the PSST-loop mutagenesis system are both capable of the comparison.

open_questions/1.rationale: The human literature is a handful of pedigrees reported one or two at a time across twenty-seven years, with no cohort study and no systematic follow-up. Age of onset, survival, and whether the optic-atrophy patients later develop basal ganglia disease are all unknown. The sibling entity NDUFA12 turned out to require visual surveillance in patients who presented with motor features alone; whether the reverse surveillance is needed here has not been asked.

open_questions/2.rationale: The dogs reproduce the clinical and imaging phenotype convincingly and supply histology no human case report offers. But the variant is canine-specific, at a residue position with no reported human counterpart, and its consequences were assessed by differential rescue in a fly rather than by measuring complex I in the affected animals. The model may therefore be recapitulating Leigh syndrome as a syndrome while diverging from the specific molecular lesion of human MC1DN3.

evidence.snippet: we describe a heterozygous de novo variant (c.205C>T; p.(Arg69*)) in the integral cohesin structural protein, STAG2. This variant is associated with decreased STAG2 protein expression.
evidence.explanation: Identifies a de novo truncating STAG2 variant with reduced protein as the causal lesion.

evidence.snippet: Herein, we suggest that STAG2 is a dosage-sensitive gene and that heterozygous loss-of-function variants lead to a cohesinopathy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes STAG2 dosage sensitivity and loss-of-function as the disease mechanism.

steps/2.description: The initiating lesion is a germline (or somatic-mosaic) loss-of-function STAG2 variant. STAG2 encodes an integral, dosage-sensitive subunit of the cohesin complex; heterozygous de novo truncating variants reduce STAG2 protein and produce a cohesinopathy, establishing STAG2 as haploinsufficient for neurodevelopment.

evidence.snippet: The cohesin complex is an evolutionarily conserved multi-subunit protein complex which regulates sister chromatid cohesion during mitosis and meiosis. Additionally, the cohesin complex regulates DNA replication, DNA repair, and transcription.
evidence.explanation: Defines the functions of cohesin that STAG2 deficiency perturbs.

steps/3.description: Reduced STAG2 lowers the amount of intact, functional cohesin. The cohesin complex is a conserved multi-subunit ring that mediates sister chromatid cohesion and organizes chromatin; STAG2 is one of two mutually exclusive HEAT-repeat subunits (STAG1/STAG2) that direct cohesin to genomic loci.

evidence.snippet: The analyses of metaphase spreads did not exhibit premature sister chromatid separation; however, delayed sister chromatid cohesion was observed.
evidence.explanation: Directly documents the delayed sister chromatid cohesion phenotype in patient cells.

steps/4.description: A measurable cellular consequence of STAG2 deficiency: patient-cell metaphase spreads show delayed sister chromatid cohesion kinetics rather than overt premature sister chromatid separation. This subtle, non-catastrophic cohesion defect is consistent with the view that the developmental phenotype arises from cohesin's regulatory (transcription / genome organization) roles rather than from mitotic cohesion failure.

evidence.snippet: they exhibited altered cell cycle profiles and gene expression patterns that were consistent with cohesin deficiency
evidence.explanation: Directly links STAG2 deficiency to altered gene-expression programs, the proposed developmental effector.

evidence.snippet: STAG2, which encodes a subunit of the cohesin complex responsible for chromosomal segregation and transcriptional regulation
evidence.explanation: Identifies transcriptional regulation as a core cohesin function disrupted in MKMS.

steps/5.description: The developmental phenotype of STAG2-associated cohesinopathy is attributed primarily to cohesin's non-mitotic roles: regulation of transcription and three-dimensional genome/chromatin organization. Loss of STAG2-cohesin perturbs gene-expression programs required for normal development.

steps/1.description: LIPT2 encodes lipoyltransferase 2, which transfers octanoyl groups from octanoyl-ACP (synthesized by the mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis system) to the glycine cleavage system H protein (GCSH). This is the first committed step in the mitochondrial lipoylation pathway. The octanoyl-GCSH is then converted to lipoyl-GCSH by lipoic acid synthetase (LIAS), and LIPT1 relays lipoyl groups from GCSH to the E2 subunits of alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenases. Loss-of-function mutations in LIPT2 abolish this initial transfer, leading to deficient lipoylation of all lipoic acid-dependent enzyme complexes and disruption of the glycine cleavage system. Unlike LIPT1 deficiency which spares glycine cleavage, LIPT2 deficiency affects all lipoylated proteins.

steps/2.description: Defective lipoylation of the E2 subunits of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDHc), alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (alpha-KGDHc), and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase (BCKDHc) impairs oxidative metabolism of pyruvate, alpha-ketoglutarate, and branched-chain amino acids. Loss of PDHc blocks entry of glycolytic end products into the TCA cycle, causing pyruvate and lactate accumulation and energy failure. Loss of alpha-KGDHc disrupts the TCA cycle at its midpoint. The brain is particularly vulnerable due to its high dependence on oxidative metabolism.

evidence.snippet: Iron dyshomeostasis with iron overload is associated with increased production of radical oxygen species and oxidative stress, protein misfolding and aggregation, dysfunction of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway, neuroinflammation and ferroptosis (iron-dependent apoptosis)
evidence.explanation: This directly supports oxidative and related injury pathways downstream of iron dyshomeostasis.

edges/5.description: Iron dyshomeostasis promotes oxidative stress and other neuronal injury pathways.

evidence.snippet: NBIA disorders comprise a group of rare but devastating inherited neurological diseases with unifying features of progressive cognitive and motor decline, and increased iron deposition in the basal ganglia.
evidence.explanation: This directly links basal-ganglia iron deposition with progressive cognitive and motor decline in NBIA.

edges/6.description: Neuronal injury in basal ganglia and related networks drives progressive neurologic decline.

evidence.snippet: PKAN is caused by a mutation in the PANK2 gene on chromosome 20 which encodes the pantothenate kinase 2 enzyme.
evidence.explanation: This directly identifies PANK2 as causal for PKAN.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic PANK2 variants disrupt mitochondrial pantothenate kinase activity.

evidence.snippet: Phospholipase-associated neurodegeneration (PLAN) caused by mutations in the PLA2G6 gene is a rare neurodegenerative disorder that presents with four sub-groups.
evidence.explanation: This directly identifies PLA2G6 as causal for PLAN.

genes/1.notes: PLA2G6 variants cause PLAN/INAD and dystonia-parkinsonism phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: MPAN is a monogenic NBIA disorder caused by mutations in the C19orf12 gene on chromosome 19.
evidence.explanation: This directly identifies C19orf12 as causal for MPAN.

evidence.snippet: BPAN is caused by de novo mutations in the WDR45 gene located on the X chromosome.
evidence.explanation: This directly identifies WDR45 as causal for BPAN.

evidence.snippet: Treatment for NBIA disorders remains symptomatic but a placebo-controlled double-blind study is underway.
evidence.explanation: This review supports symptomatic management as the established care baseline.

treatments/0.description: Current routine management remains largely symptomatic, addressing movement disorder, spasticity, speech/swallowing needs, and functional support.

evidence.snippet: demonstrating radiological improvement with reduction of iron load in the basal ganglia and a trend to slowing of disease progression.
evidence.explanation: This supports deferiprone as potentially disease-modifying but not definitively curative.

evidence.snippet: Our results show the progressive decrease in the cerebral accumulation of iron evaluated by MRI and a substantial stability of the overall clinical neurological picture without a significant correlation between clinical and radiological findings.
evidence.explanation: This long-term cohort supports MRI iron reduction and clinical stability, with the caveat that radiologic and clinical outcomes did not correlate significantly.

treatments/1.description: Deferiprone is an investigational or off-label disease-modifying strategy aimed at lowering brain iron; evidence supports radiologic improvement and possible clinical stabilization in subsets rather than broad cure.

evidence.snippet: A general mechanistic approach for treatment of NBIA disorders is with iron chelators which bind and remove iron.
evidence.explanation: This supports the target mechanism for iron chelation therapy.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Deferiprone is intended to chelate brain iron.

treatments/2.description: CoA-Z is an investigational PKAN substrate-bypass strategy intended to address PANK2-related CoA biosynthesis deficiency.
